title: Concurrency & Multi-Node Testing
description: Races, deadlocks, distributed failure modes, and how to test them in SDK labs

questions.scenario: A C++ SDK call graph shares a connection pool. Stress tests pass with 2 threads and fail with 64 threads with corrupted headers — only on release builds.
questions.question: What class of bug is most likely, and what is your first instrumentation idea?
questions.modelAnswer: Data race / missing synchronization — run under ThreadSanitizer (or add targeted locking assertions) and stress with more threads/cores.
questions.explanation: Release-only corruption under concurrency screams races; TSAN and targeted sync checks are the usual first moves.

questions.question: What does a data race mean?
options: Concurrent conflicting accesses to a memory location with no happens-before relation
Two Jenkins agents picking the same label
A TCP retransmission after packet loss
A Docker layer failing to compress
questions.explanation: Data races are undefined behavior in C/C++ and a top concurrency defect class.

questions.question: Complete this function so two threads increment counter 100000 times each safely using a Lock. Return the counter.
questions.explanation: The increment must be atomic w.r.t. other threads — a Lock (or atomic) protects the critical section.

questions.question: Thread A holds lock L1 and waits for L2. Thread B holds L2 and waits for L1. Name the bug and one prevention strategy.
questions.modelAnswer: Deadlock — impose a global lock ordering (always acquire L1 before L2) or use try-lock with backoff.
questions.explanation: Classic circular wait; ordering breaks the cycle.

questions.scenario: Multi-node test: Node1 sends messages to Node2. Randomly, Node2 drops for 30s then returns. The SDK sometimes never recovers subscriptions.
questions.question: What failure mode should your test inject, and what recovery property should you assert?
questions.modelAnswer: Inject network partition/disconnect; assert reconnect/resubscribe within a bound and no stuck “half-open” state.
questions.explanation: Distributed SDKs must be tested under partitions — recovery liveness is the product requirement.

questions.question: Why are sleeps (time.sleep(2)) a weak synchronization strategy in tests?
options: They are timing-dependent, slow, and still race on loaded CI machines
They always deadlock the kernel scheduler
They are forbidden by the Python language grammar
questions.explanation: Prefer condition variables, polling with timeout on a state oracle, or deterministic schedules.

questions.question: In C++, which header/facility is commonly used for a mutual-exclusion lock? Write an include and a std::mutex variable named m.
questions.explanation: std::mutex from <mutex> is the standard exclusive lock primitive.

questions.question: Define “heisenbug” in the context of concurrent SDK testing.
questions.modelAnswer: A bug that changes or disappears when observed (logging/debugger), often timing/race related.
questions.explanation: Heisenbugs dominate concurrency labs — prefer low-overhead detectors (TSAN) and record/replay.

questions.scenario: Performance validation across 16 nodes shows p99 latency spikes only when all nodes start traffic in the same millisecond.
questions.question: What test-harness change would better reveal (or avoid) synchronized thundering-herd artifacts?
questions.modelAnswer: Stagger/ramp start times with jitter and include warm-up; also measure under both synchronized and staggered patterns intentionally.
questions.explanation: Multi-node tests must control arrival processes — herds can amplify control-plane storms.

questions.question: ThreadSanitizer (TSan) is primarily designed to find…
options: Data races in native multithreaded code
CSS layout bugs in web UIs
BGP route leaks between autonomous systems
questions.explanation: TSan is a dynamic race detector for C/C++ (and similar) binaries.

questions.question: Using concurrent.futures, write code that runs work(i) for i in 0..3 in a thread pool and collects results into a list named results.
acceptedAnswers:
with ThreadPoolExecutor() as ex:
    futs = [ex.submit(work, i) for i in range(4)]
    results = [f.result() for f in futs]
questions.modelAnswer:
with ThreadPoolExecutor() as ex:
    results = list(ex.map(work, range(4)))
questions.explanation: Thread pools are a practical way to generate concurrency in Python harnesses.

questions.question: Give one invariant you could assert in a multi-producer multi-consumer queue test.
questions.modelAnswer: e.g. every enqueued item is dequeued exactly once (no loss/duplication); or sum(in)==sum(out).
questions.explanation: Conservation/ordering oracles catch subtle concurrency bugs better than spot checks.

followUpQuestions.question: Circular lock wait is called a…
Why are fixed sleeps brittle in concurrent tests?
followUpQuestions.explanation: They encode timing assumptions that fail under load.

followUpQuestions.question: Import the standard Lock type from threading.
Name one multi-node failure you should inject on purpose.
followUpQuestions.explanation: Partitions, kills, latency, loss — chaos with assertions.

tutorial.intro: Learn concurrency and multi-node failure modes with clear definitions, then practice the tools and oracles used to catch them.

levels.title: Basics
levels.tagline: Races, locks, deadlocks — with working snippets
levels.html:
Data race: two threads access the same memory, at least one write, no happens-before (lock/atomic/join). In C++ this is undefined behavior.

import threading
counter = 0
lock = threading.Lock()

def worker():
    global counter
    for _ in range(100000):
        with lock:
            counter += 1
  • threading.Lock() — mutual exclusion primitive.
  • with lock: — acquire on enter, release on exit (even if exception).
  • counter += 1 — must be inside the lock; it is read-modify-write, not atomic.
Deadlock

Thread A holds L1 waits for L2; B holds L2 waits for L1. Prevent with a global lock order (always acquire L1 before L2).

See the race without a lock

# BAD: remove the lock and rerun — final counter often < 200000
# That missing count *is* the race teaching moment.
python3 race_demo.py
python3 race_demo.py
Run your two-thread increment demo; compare locked vs unlocked results.

levels.title: Advanced
levels.html:
Heisenbug: disappears or changes when you add prints/debugger — usually timing/race related.

g++ -fsanitize=thread -g -O1 main.cpp -o main && ./main
-fsanitize=thread
Compile/link with ThreadSanitizer (TSan) to detect data races at runtime.
-g
Debug symbols for useful stack traces.
-O1
Some optimization; TSan docs recommend avoiding heavy -O3 at first.
sleep(2) in tests

Fixed sleeps are timing assumptions. Prefer waiting on a condition/event with a timeout, or poll a state oracle.

Invariant example: every enqueued item is dequeued exactly once (conservation).

export TSAN_OPTIONS=halt_on_error=1
TSAN_OPTIONS
Runtime config for ThreadSanitizer.
halt_on_error=1
Stop on first race report (useful in CI).
Fix order

Increase concurrency → run under TSan → fix races → only then add lightweight logging. Logging first can hide races (heisenbug).

levels.title: Expert
levels.html:
• Inject disconnect/partition; assert reconnect/resubscribe within an SLO.
  • Stagger multi-node starts with jitter — synchronized herds amplify storms.
  • Report p99/p999 with pinned CPUs; averages hide tail latency.
python -c "import time,random; time.sleep(random.uniform(0,2))"
random.uniform(0,2)
Example jitter delay before starting a node role — avoid thundering herds.
Experienced line

“We chaos-test recovery and treat liveness as a first-class assertion.”

tc qdisc add dev eth0 root netem delay 100ms loss 1%
tc qdisc add
Add a traffic-control queueing discipline (needs root/net_admin).
dev eth0
Interface to impair.
root netem
Network emulator.
delay 100ms loss 1%
Inject latency and packet loss for recovery testing.

Always remove netem after the lab (tc qdisc del dev eth0 root) or you will confuse the next job.
